newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Chirac hails Clinton over Zaire.
newsitem.headline: France's Chirac hails Clinton over Zaire.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac, who has been pushing to send a multinational force including U.S. troops to Zaire, on Friday welcomed President Bill Clinton's tentative decision to participate.
Chirac said in a statement that the force, intended to protect and ensure relief for more than one million refugees, was still needed although refuges were streaming home to Rwanda.

"France warmly welcomes the announcement by President Clinton of the decision in principle to participate to the multinational force which will carry out an emergency humanitarian intervention in eastern Zaire," he said.
"France hopes that the Security Council's imminent decision will allow for the deployment, as soon as possible, of the multinational force which remains fully needed," he said.
Clinton said on Friday reports that Rwandan refugees were returning home from Zaire were "a hopeful sign" but Washington remained prepared to contribute troops.
He said it would be premature to conclude that the mass return might eliminate the need for the relief mission.
Chirac said he had discussed the situation in eastern Zaire in detail with Clinton in a telephone conversation on Thursday.

He said Paris, Washington and their alies would help central African states find a lasting solution to the region's problems in a proposed international conference sponsored by the United Nations and the Organisation of African Unity.

Washington announced earlier this week it had agreed tentatively to send 1,000 troops to Goma, Zaire, to secure the airport and set up a protected corridor so refugees can return to Rwanda, with another 3,000 U.S. troops or so providing support from neighbouring countries.
France plans to contribute up to 2,000 troops to the Canadian-led mission, which could total 10,000 men following expected authorisation by the U.N. Security Council.
A French foreign ministry official told reporters initial planning was that United States and Canadian troops would operate in the Goma area while European contingents would be based at Bukavu.
Both airfields are now in the hands of Tutsi Banyamulenge rebels who have warned they will shoot at the French on sight and have also been cool about the arrival of other contingents.
